birthright.name: Consulate of the Sea
birthright.text: Sea traders gather 20 % more, galleys build 20 % faster, and loans cost a quarter less interest.
birthright.why: Barcelona's and Valencia's sea trade ran under the Consolat de Mar, Catalan galleys sailed to Sicily and the Levant, and Valencian censals made the Crown's credit cheap.

heydays.name: The Magnanimous
heydays.text: While Naples is yours: galleys hit 20 % harder, sieges 15 % faster, and one more envoy.
heydays.why: Alfonso V conquered Naples in 1442, kept his court and fleet there and ran the Crown's Italian diplomacy from it.

heydays.name: Valencia's golden century
heydays.text: Pottery output +40 %, Valencia's trade profit +40 %, and loans cost 20 % less interest.
heydays.why: The catalogue calls Valencia a booming port and financial centre, the source of loans to Alfonso, famous for Manises ceramics.

burden.name: Pactist Corts
burden.text: Tax reaching you -10 %; levies serve one month less before pay; one official fewer without strain.
burden.why: Each realm's Corts voted taxes and could refuse them, and the king lived in Naples; the catalogue lists pactist estates and an absent king as constraints.

birthright.name: Sagres pilots
birthright.text: Ships build 15 % faster, storms sink a third fewer, sea crossings take 10 % fewer days; ports raise 20 % more sailors and fisheries feed 20 % more.
birthright.why: Under Prince Henry, pilots from Lagos near Sagres charted Madeira, the Azores and the coast past Bojador (1434) and Arguin (1443); the kingdom lived from fishing, salt and the sea.

heydays.name: Carreira da Índia
heydays.text: Traders on sea routes gather 30 % more; harbours cost a quarter less; customs officers on the coast are 20 % stronger.
heydays.why: The catalogue's 'route to India' path: the Cape rounded in 1488 and India reached in 1498, after which Lisbon's crown fleets ran the yearly India voyage.

heydays.name: Engenhos of Brazil
heydays.text: Sugar output +30 %, plantations cost a quarter less, ports offer 20 % more seafolk jobs, and the coast grows 10 % faster.
heydays.why: Madeira sugar (from the 1440s) was the model for the Brazilian captaincies and engenhos of the 1500s; inferred from the catalogue's Atlantic-island economy.

heydays.name: Gold of the Gerais
heydays.text: Gold output +40 %, loans cost 20 % less interest, and masters of works are 20 % stronger.
heydays.why: The Brazilian gold strikes of the 1690s financed Lisbon's court and building programme into the 1750s (inferred from the catalogue's Atlantic path).

burden.name: Bread from abroad
burden.text: Harvests roll one step worse and people grow 5 % slower.
burden.why: The catalogue lists a small population and a grain deficit as Portugal's constraints; the kingdom bought wheat from abroad and from Madeira.

birthright.name: Court of Granada

birthright.why: Granada was a court of scholars, judges and soldiers.

birthright.name: Armourers of Milan
birthright.text: Arms output +25 %, cloth output +20 %, and knights and lancers break 5 points later.
birthright.why: Milan's arms and armour makers and fustian weavers supplied half of Europe; its own lances fought in the best harness of the age.

heydays.name: Sforza's lances
heydays.text: Commanders may fight sforzesca; knights and lancers hit 15 % harder; hired companies cost 20 % less.
heydays.why: Francesco Sforza, the duke's son-in-law and condottiere, took Milan in 1450; the catalogue says a strong condottiere successor turns it toward consolidation.

heydays.name: The Navigli
heydays.text: Core harvests roll one step better, irrigation works cost 30 % less, wells and drains a quarter less, and 20 % more fleeing craftsmen come.
heydays.why: The Lombard plain was irrigated by the navigli canals; under Ludovico Sforza engineers including Leonardo worked on canals and the Ospedale Maggiore was built.

burden.name: Turncoat captains
burden.text: Hired companies cost 25 % more and break 5 points sooner.
burden.why: The catalogue lists unreliable condottieri and the duke's distrust of his commanders (Carmagnola, Piccinino, Sforza all changed sides).

birthright.name: Lagoon and Arsenal
birthright.text: Galleys build 30 % faster, the capital's garrison is 40 % stronger, and ports raise 15 % more sailors.
birthright.why: The Arsenal was the state shipyard producing galleys, and the catalogue notes that the lagoon made the capital nearly impregnable.

heydays.name: The mude to Alexandria
heydays.text: Sea traders gather 25 % more and customs officers are 30 % stronger.
heydays.why: State galley convoys (mude) sailed to Alexandria, Beirut, Constantinople, Flanders and England, giving Venice the spice trade.

heydays.name: Aldine presses
heydays.text: Book output +40 % and presses cost a quarter less.
heydays.why: Inferred: Venice's capital, paper trade and scholars from Padua made it Europe's largest printing centre around 1500.

heydays.name: Morosini's galleys

heydays.name: Renaissance Rome
heydays.text: Houses of worship cost 30 % less, 30 % more fleeing craftsmen and scholars choose you, and officials cost 15 % less.
heydays.why: Back in Rome from 1443, the popes rebuilt the city; the curia sold offices to pay for it (inferred from the catalogue's patronage path).

heydays.name: Tridentine reform

heydays.name: The Alfonsine court

heydays.why: Alfonso's veteran Iberian-Italian army and Catalan galleys won the kingdom by 1442; his court at Castel Nuovo drew humanists.

heydays.why: Inferred from the event tree: after the siege of Vienna in 1683 the Habsburgs reconquered Hungary up to the Treaty of Karlowitz.

heydays.text: Tribute +40 %, loot +30 %, and armies forage 20 % more.
heydays.why: The Sarai khan claimed Rus tribute (vykhod), raided Ryazan and the Oka frontier and lived from booty and ransoms (catalogue).

heydays.name: Fair of Hajji Tarkhan
heydays.text: Traders passing +25 %, river traders gather 15 % more, delta fish +20 %, tolls at Hajji Tarkhan +50 %.
heydays.why: If Rus tribute failed, the catalogue's adaptation turns the horde to the Volga trade with the Caspian, Iran and Khwarazm.

burden.name: The beys choose the khan
burden.text: Clan chiefs start a step less loyal, and you can hold 2 fewer lords.
burden.why: The qarachi beys of the leading clans made and unmade khans, and the Mangits played their own game (catalogue authority distribution and failure conditions).

birthright.name: Remounts of the steppe
birthright.text: Horses breed 40 % faster, herds grow 20 % faster, horse archers hit 15 % harder on grassland, and armies march 15 % faster.
birthright.why: Crimean Khanate's strength was its herds and its riders.

heydays.name: The last great ride
heydays.text: Horse archers hit 20 % harder, loot +40 %, recruits refill 20 % faster, until you learn massed hand guns.
heydays.why: Inferred: steppe armies kept their edge until gunpowder infantry and field guns spread.

heydays.name: Cattle wealth
heydays.text: Herds grow 35 % faster, horses 25 % faster, recruits refill 20 % faster.
heydays.why: Inferred: herding peoples grew strong in good grazing years.

burden.name: Divided ulus
burden.text: Lords start a step less loyal and officials take a year longer to settle in.
burden.why: Steppe power was shared among clans and princes (catalogue constraints).

birthright.name: Tribes of the Dasht-i Qipchaq
birthright.text: Recruits refill 20 % faster, horses +25 %, herds grow 12 % faster, and armies forage 25 % more.
birthright.why: Abu'l-Khayr led some two dozen Uzbek tribes with large herds between the Tura and the Aral Sea, raising cavalry by tribal levy and booty (catalogue).

heydays.name: Towns of the Syr Darya
heydays.text: Sieges 20 % faster, conquests alarm neighbours 15 % less, Foreign rule fades 20 % sooner, market folk jobs +20 %.
heydays.why: In 1446 Abu'l-Khayr took Sighnaq, Arquq, Suzaq, Uzgend and Aq-Qorghan, some by surrender, and made Sighnaq his seat (catalogue).

heydays.name: Shaybani's Bukhara
heydays.text: Madrasa seats +25 %, tax collectors 20 % stronger, horse archers deal 20 % more hits.
heydays.why: Muhammad Shaybani took Samarkand and Herat in 1500-1507 and the Uzbek khanates ruled Transoxiana for four centuries (catalogue future path).

burden.name: Beys who can ride away
burden.text: Clan chiefs start a step less loyal, and you can support 2 fewer officials.
burden.why: A loose tribal confederation with little administrative apparatus, whose beys could follow another prince; the Kazakh secession came from this (catalogue constraints).

birthright.name: Barracks of the Citadel
birthright.text: Mamluk horse archers break 8 points later and deal 12 % more hits; commanders risen from the ranks start with +1 Might.
birthright.why: Slave boys bought mainly from the Circassian coast were trained in barracks schools of the Cairo Citadel into the formidable heavy cavalry archers the catalogue describes.

heydays.name: Pepper of Jidda
heydays.text: Customs officers 40 % stronger, coastal tolls +40 %, Egyptian trade +15 %.
heydays.why: Barsbay's pepper and sugar monopolies and the customs of Alexandria and Jidda were the regime's richest revenues while the spice route ran through the Red Sea.

heydays.name: Waqf of the Nile
heydays.text: Houses of worship and castles cost a quarter less, masters of works 20 % stronger, Egypt's harvests one step better.
heydays.why: The irrigated Nile valley and the great cities are the catalogue's base; late Mamluk sultans' building of mosques, madrasas and forts is inferred from that wealth.

burden.name: Each sultan his own mamluks
burden.text: Lords start a step less loyal, and recruits refill 15 % slower while new slave soldiers must be bought abroad.
burden.why: Each sultan built his own household and succession passed through faction fights; the army depended on buying slave boys via Genoese Black Sea ports (catalogue constraints).

birthright.name: Kitabkhana of Herat
birthright.text: Scholars make 12 % more research, school seats +25 %, officials reach full effect a year sooner, and fleeing scholars favour you.
birthright.why: Under Shah Rukh and Gawhar Shad, Herat became the cultural capital of the Persianate world, with an experienced Persian fiscal bureaucracy (catalogue).

heydays.name: Ulugh Beg's observatory
heydays.text: Observatories, universities and lenses cost 20 % less to research, scholars +10 %, spread discount cap +8.
heydays.why: Ulugh Beg ruled Transoxiana from Samarkand, seat of his observatory and madrasas (catalogue key locations).

heydays.name: Khorasan highway
heydays.text: Traders passing +25 %, land traders gather 15 % more, caravanserais cost a quarter less.
heydays.why: The realm sat on the overland Silk Road Samarkand-Herat-Tabriz and the Herat-Qandahar-Multan road to India, and depended on peace along it.

heydays.name: Mirzas in Hindustan
heydays.text: Commanders may take the Rumi dastur, guns deal 15 % more hits, and you can hold 2 more lords.
heydays.why: A Timurid prince, Babur, driven from Transoxiana by the Uzbeks, turned through Kabul to India (catalogue future path); this heyday is inferred from that line.

burden.name: Every prince an army
burden.text: Appanage princes rule their own courts: lords start a step less loyal and provinces are 20 % further from the throne.
burden.why: Grandsons held Fars, Iraq-i Ajam and Gurgan with their own armies and Ulugh Beg ruled Transoxiana almost alone; succession went by contest (catalogue constraints).

birthright.name: Remounts of the steppe

birthright.why: Moghulistan's strength was its herds and its riders.

birthright.name: Herds of the Four Oirat
birthright.text: Horses +30 %, horse archers break 6 points later, grassland marches 20 % faster, armies forage 15 % more.
birthright.why: Every nomadic household rode to war, and Esen's cavalry was mobile enough to beat Ming field armies; wealth lay in horses (catalogue).

heydays.name: Esen's tribute missions
heydays.text: Land traders gather 20 % more, tribute +25 %, loot +30 %.
heydays.why: Esen enlarged tribute missions to Beijing and redistributed Ming goods and loot to his followers (catalogue).

heydays.name: The Dzungar khanate
heydays.text: Powder mills may be built early, tribute +25 %, and you can hold 2 more lords.
heydays.why: The catalogue notes the Oirat revived as the Dzungar Khanate in the 17th century; Galdan made Altishahr tributary in 1680 (event tree).

burden.name: A taishi, not a khan
burden.text: Legitimacy −10, and clan chiefs start a step less loyal.
burden.why: Esen ruled as taishi behind a Chinggisid figurehead; his non-Chinggisid legitimacy is a catalogue vulnerability, and his usurpation ended in murder in 1455.

birthright.name: Jinshi of the metropolitan examinations
birthright.text: The realm supports 3 more officials, officials reach full effect a year sooner, and their wages cost 10 % less.
birthright.why: The Ming governed through a very large literate bureaucracy recruited by examination, with ministries in Beijing and a parallel set in Nanjing.

heydays.name: Yu Qian's defence of the capital
heydays.text: Garrisons fight 30 % harder, castles cost a fifth less, and commanders may fight in the wagon-fort style.
heydays.why: After Tumu (1449) Yu Qian held Beijing; the northern garrisons at Datong and Xuanfu and the later border walls became the Ming answer to steppe cavalry.

heydays.name: Jingdezhen blue-and-white
heydays.text: Porcelain output rises 40 %, and Jiangnan's silk looms make 40 % more.
heydays.why: Jingdezhen porcelain and Jiangnan silk were the goods Asia and later Europe wanted most from China.

heydays.name: The Single Whip in silver
heydays.text: 15 % more tax reaches you, tax collectors are 20 % stronger, and Heavy taxes does not count in core provinces.
heydays.why: As Japanese and American silver poured in, Zhang Juzheng's 1570s-80s reforms folded land tax and labour service into one silver payment (inferred fit to this age).

burden.name: The sea ban
burden.text: Traders on sea routes gather 20 % less, and ports raise 10 % fewer sailors.
burden.why: Private overseas trade stayed banned (haijin) after 1433; trade was limited to tribute missions while smuggling and piracy grew.

birthright.name: Hall of Worthies
birthright.text: Scholars research 15 % more, officials reach full effect a year sooner, the realm supports 2 more officials, and Ming thinks a step better of you.
birthright.why: Sejong's Jiphyeonjeon and a centrally appointed, examination-recruited officialdom made Joseon's administration very strong for its size; correct tribute kept Ming close.

heydays.name: Rain gauges and the Farmer's Talk
heydays.text: Core harvests roll a step better, stores rot a quarter less, Hungry does not count in the core, 10 % more core tax arrives, tax collectors +15 %.
heydays.why: Standard rain gauges (1441), farm manuals and the graded Gongbeop land tax of 1444 were Sejong's tools against drought and uneven assessment.

heydays.name: Turtle ships and righteous armies
heydays.text: Turtle ships hit 30 % harder, commanders may use the hwacha battery, and foreign rule lasts 30 % longer in your homeland.
heydays.why: In the Imjin War (1592-1598) Yi Sun-sin's armoured ships, hwacha rocket carts and the volunteer righteous armies wore down the Japanese invasion.

heydays.name: Uniform tribute law
heydays.text: 15 % more tax reaches you, Heavy taxes does not count anywhere, and officials cost 10 % less.
heydays.why: The Daedongbeop (1608-1708) turned county tribute into a land tax in rice and the 1750 equal-service law halved the cloth levy; this is the later Joseon revival (inferred fit to this age).

burden.name: The commoner's service
burden.text: Recruits refill 15 % slower, levies serve a month less before pay, and 5 % less tax reaches you.
burden.why: Military and corvee service fell on commoner men while yangban escaped it, and evasion was growing; Joseon was not organised for large wars.

birthright.name: Village registers
birthright.text: Tax reach +10 %, tax collectors +20 %, recruits refill 15 % faster and levies serve 2 months more before pay.
birthright.why: The Lê state rebuilt village commune registers for land, tax and soldiers, and let its peasant soldiers farm in rotation.

heydays.name: Hồng Đức court
heydays.text: Two more officials, officials reach full effect a year sooner, school seats +30 % and scholars +10 %.
heydays.why: Lê Thánh Tông (r.1460-97) built a Confucian bureaucratic state staffed through examinations and gave it the Hồng Đức law code.

heydays.name: Nam tiến
heydays.text: Conquests settle 25 % faster, frontier growth +15 %, the tongue spreads 25 % faster and frontier land harvests one step better.
heydays.why: Inferred from the catalogue's southern path: Viet settlers and the Nguyễn lords pushed south past Champa into the Mekong delta through the 1600s-1700s.

heydays.name: The villages fight
heydays.text: Guerrilla style, foreign rule in your homeland lasts 40 % longer, light troops hit 25 % harder in jungle and recruits refill 10 % faster.
heydays.why: Inferred: the memory of the anti-Ming war and the commune villages, which the catalogue names as sources of cohesion, carried into the resistance to French conquest in the 1880s.

burden.name: Thanh Hóa grandees
burden.text: Two fewer officials before strain; noble lords start one step less loyal.
burden.why: The Lam Sơn 'founding meritorious officials' dominated a court of regents and purges; the catalogue names court coup or regicide as a failure condition.

birthright.name: Sailors of the South China Sea
birthright.text: Ships build 25 % faster, ports raise 45 % more sailors, and fisheries feed 30 % more.
birthright.why: Champa faced the South China Sea; its coasts lived from fishing and shipping.

heydays.name: Open ocean
heydays.text: Sea crossings 25 % shorter, ships build 25 % faster, traders at sea gather 25 % more.
heydays.why: Inferred: seafaring realms gained most when ocean sailing spread.

heydays.name: Hired valour
heydays.text: Hired companies cost 30 % less, levies break 5 points later, recruits refill 30 % faster.
heydays.why: Inferred: mountain peoples sold their soldiering when armies grew.

burden.name: Thin soil
burden.text: Harvests roll a step worse at home and the people grow 10 % slower.
burden.why: Inferred from the catalogue's reliance on the sea over farmland.

birthright.why: The Mekong carried Lan Xang's grain and trade.

birthright.name: Island of three rivers
birthright.text: The capital's garrison +40 %, river land harvests one step better, capital trade +15 %, market folk jobs +20 % and traders on the coast +15 %.
birthright.why: Ayutthaya sat on an island ringed by the Chao Phraya, Pa Sak and Lopburi, protected by floods and fed by floating rice, and was an entrepôt for China, the Malay world and the Bay of Bengal.

heydays.name: Trailok's ranks
heydays.text: Two more officials, muster masters +30 %, troop cap +0.5 points and officials reach full effect a year sooner.
heydays.why: Trailokanat (r.1448-88) reorganised ministries and ranked every subject by land (sakdina), ruling from Phitsanulok during the Lan Na war.

heydays.name: Narai's open port
heydays.text: One more trader, sea traders gather 20 % more and one more envoy.
heydays.why: Inferred from the catalogue's royal trade monopolies: under Narai (1656-88) Ayutthaya hosted Dutch, French, Persian and Japanese merchants and sent embassies as far as Versailles.

heydays.name: Bamboo in the wind
heydays.text: Inventions cost 15 % less, tax collectors +20 % and one more envoy while you keep your independence.
heydays.why: Inferred: Siam, heir of Ayutthaya's court, kept its independence by treaty and Chulalongkorn's reforms while its neighbours were colonised.

burden.name: Princes of the palace
burden.text: All lords start one step less loyal and legitimacy is 10 lower.
burden.why: The catalogue names a succession tradition prone to conflict and princely governors with their own retinues; succession wars recur through Ayutthaya's history.

birthright.name: Kyaukse weirs
birthright.text: Core lands harvest one step better, irrigation works cost 30 % less, stores rot 30 % less, core rice +20 % and recruits refill 15 % faster.
birthright.why: Ava's power rested on the old irrigated granaries of Kyaukse and Minbu, worked by crown service groups (ahmudan) who also filled the levies.

heydays.name: The Bhamo road
heydays.text: While at peace with the Ming: Ming opinion +1, one more envoy, traders passing the frontier +30 % and horses bred +20 %.
heydays.why: Invested by the Ming as Ava-Burma, Ava bargained over the captured Möng Mao ruler and traded cotton for Yunnan silver and horses along the Irrawaddy to Bhamo.

heydays.name: Sawbwa horse, Burman foot
heydays.text: Shan clan chiefs start one step more loyal, lords bring 25 % more men, horse hits 20 % harder in hills and conquests settle 20 % faster.
heydays.why: Ava's reconquest of Mohnyin, Kale and Mogaung (1439-42) relied on loyal Shan lords like Thihapate; its armies joined Shan cavalry to Burman infantry.

burden.name: Princely governors
burden.text: Noble lords start one step less loyal and every province is 20 % further from Ava.
burden.why: Appanage governors of Prome, Toungoo and Yamethin kept their own retinues and revolted repeatedly; the catalogue names governor revolts as Ava's failure condition.

birthright.name: Brantas sawah
birthright.text: Core lands harvest one step better, rice +25 %, growth +10 % and rice paddies cost 10 % less.
birthright.why: Majapahit ruled the volcanic rice plains of the Brantas and Solo, the largest rice surplus and population in the archipelago.

heydays.name: Fleets of jong
heydays.text: Junks build 20 % faster, 20 % more sailors and tribute +25 %.
heydays.why: Port contingents of Javanese jong once carried Majapahit's tribute claims across the archipelago; the catalogue gives reuniting the court and reasserting maritime authority as its opportunity.

heydays.name: Ports of the pasisir
heydays.text: Coastal trade +20 %, coastal traders passing +25 %, sea traders gather 15 % more and customs officers +10 %.
heydays.why: Tuban, Gresik and Surabaya traded rice, salt and Maluku spices to Malacca and China; holding them kept that wealth in the court's hands.

burden.name: Bhre appanages
burden.text: Noble lords start one step less loyal and bring 20 % fewer men.
burden.why: Royal appanage holders (bhre) ruled provinces and became rivals, as in the Paregreg war; the catalogue names civil war among princes as a failure condition.

birthright.name: Four shahbandars
birthright.text: Traders passing the capital +30 %, customs officers +30 %, capital trade +20 % and 20 % more fleeing market folk choose you.
birthright.why: Malacca drew Gujarati, Tamil, Javanese, Ryukyuan and Chinese traders with a safe harbour and fixed dues run by four harbourmasters (shahbandars), one per group of merchant nations.

heydays.name: Orang Laut fleets
heydays.text: Galleys hit 20 % harder, 20 % more sailors and tribute +25 %.
heydays.why: The sea people of Riau-Lingga manned the ruler's fleet by personal loyalty; under Muzaffar and Mansur Shah it coerced the coasts of the Strait into tribute.

heydays.name: A lamp on the strait
heydays.text: Faith spreads 30 % faster, same-faith countries think one step better of you, 20 % more fleeing scholars choose you and school seats +20 %.
heydays.why: Malacca's conversion tied it to Muslim Indian Ocean merchants and made it a centre from which Islam spread through the archipelago.

burden.name: Sons of rival mothers
burden.text: Legitimacy 10 lower; merchant-house lords start one step less loyal.
burden.why: Court factions backing princes of rival royal mothers fought over the throne in 1444-46, and the catalogue warns a succession war drives merchants away.

birthright.why: The Brunei river carried Brunei's grain and trade.

birthright.name: Delta of muslin and rice
birthright.text: Cloth is made 30 % faster, river tiles harvest one step better, and ships build 15 % faster.
birthright.why: The catalogue names immense agricultural and textile wealth (rice, fine cotton muslin, silk) and shipbuilding on the shifting rivers of the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta.

heydays.name: Tanka of the Bay
heydays.text: Traders on sea routes gather 25 % more; customs officers on the coast are 40 % stronger.
heydays.why: Chittagong and Satgaon linked Bengal's silver tanka to Pegu, Malacca, Sumatra and Ceylon; the Bay of Bengal trade was underway in 1444.

heydays.name: Husain Shahi court
heydays.text: Wrong faith no longer stirs your provinces; scholars work 10 % better and judges are 20 % stronger.
heydays.why: Hindu landholders and officials served a Muslim ruling class; under the Husain Shahis (from 1494) the court patronised Bengali letters (inferred from the catalogue's later path).

heydays.name: Looms of Sonargaon
heydays.text: Traders passing your provinces rise 25 %, silk output 20 %, and coastal trade profit 15 %.
heydays.why: Bengal's export textiles drew the world's merchants to the delta; the catalogue lists Sonargaon and silk among its cities and goods.

burden.name: Sultans made by the guard
burden.text: Legitimacy -10, and officials cost 15 % more in wages.
burden.why: The catalogue's constraint is noble factions and its failure condition a court coup: nobles killed and installed sultans in the 1430s, and Habshi guards seized the throne 1487-1494.

birthright.name: Horses through Dabhol and Chaul
birthright.text: Horses bred +25 %; horsemen hold 10 points longer and hit 10 % harder.
birthright.why: The catalogue lists strong cavalry with access to imported horses through the Konkan ports of Chaul and Dabhol, and an open plateau that favours cavalry.

heydays.name: Gawan's eight tarafs
heydays.text: Tax collectors 30 % stronger, officials reach full effect a year sooner, tax reaching you +10 %.
heydays.why: The catalogue's reform path: the minister Mahmud Gawan subdivided the provinces in the 1460s-1470s to curb the governors.

heydays.name: Gharib newcomers
heydays.text: 50 % more fleeing scholars choose you, sea traders gather 15 % more, and Shia lands think better of you.
heydays.why: Persian, Arab and Turkic 'Afaqi' immigrants arrived through the Persian Gulf and Red Sea trade of the Konkan ports.

burden.name: Deccani against Gharib
burden.text: Nobles start one step less loyal, officials cost 10 % more, and lords bring 10 % fewer men.
burden.why: The catalogue names factionalism as the main constraint: Deccani and Afaqi factions competed for office, and a factional massacre followed the Konkan disaster of c.1447.

birthright.name: City of Victory
birthright.text: Irrigation works cost 30 % less, dryland tiles harvest one step better, the capital's garrison +30 %, +2 lords supported.
birthright.why: A fortified granite capital on the Tungabhadra fed by tank and channel irrigation, ruling through amaranayaka chiefs who held land for service.

heydays.name: Deva Raya's horse archers
heydays.text: Horse archers hold 10 points longer, horses bred +20 %, hired companies cost 20 % less.
heydays.why: Deva Raya II (1424-1446) enrolled Muslim cavalry and archers and expanded horse imports through the west coast ports.

heydays.name: Court of Krishnadevaraya
heydays.text: Scholars work 10 % better, tribute +25 %, prestige +1.
heydays.why: With the largest revenue base in the peninsula and tribute from southern chiefs, the kingdom peaked under Krishnadevaraya (1509-1529), a patron of Telugu letters (inferred).

burden.name: Horses from overseas
burden.text: Horses bred -30 %, and horsemen break 4 points sooner.
burden.why: The catalogue's first constraint is horse imports: cavalry quality was limited by a supply that depended on foreign merchants and the west coast ports.

birthright.name: Vanias of Cambay
birthright.text: One more trader, loan interest -30 %, coastal customs officers +40 %, coastal traffic +10 %.
birthright.why: Cambay was a hub of Indian Ocean trade, and Hindu and Jain merchant and banking castes ran revenue and port administration for the sultans.

heydays.name: Begada's guns
heydays.text: Sieges 25 % faster, tribute +20 %, loot +20 %.
heydays.why: The catalogue's path: Mahmud Begada took Junagadh (1472) and Champaner (1484) after his predecessors failed before hill forts.

heydays.name: Malik Ayaz at Diu
heydays.text: Ships hit 20 % harder, galleys build 15 % faster, Diu's garrison +30 %, sailors +10 %.
heydays.why: Gujarat's naval role grew late in the century; it fought the Portuguese off Diu in 1508-1509 with Mamluk help (catalogue path).

heydays.name: Countinghouses of the gulf
heydays.text: Trade profit +15 %, sea traders gather 15 % more, 20 % more fleeing market folk choose you.
heydays.why: Merchant capital and banking are among Gujarat's strengths; its ports kept trading with Aden, Hormuz and Malacca across centuries (inferred).

burden.name: Hill forts mock the plain
burden.text: Sieges 20 % slower and tribute 15 % lower.

birthright.name: Shadiabad, the crossroads
birthright.text: Toll gold +40 %, marches 10 % faster, Mandu's garrison +30 %, recruits refill 10 % faster.
birthright.why: Routes from the Ganga plain to Gujarat and the Deccan pass through Malwa; Mandu was a plateau fortress capital, and the land fertile black soil.

heydays.name: Khalji's seasons of war
heydays.text: Levies serve 2 months longer unpaid, forage +25 %, loot +30 %, recruits refill 10 % faster.
heydays.why: Mahmud Khalji (r.1436-1469) campaigned against Delhi, Mewar, Gujarat and the Bahmanis; the catalogue calls Malwa highly mobile and aggressive.

heydays.name: Chanderi weavers
heydays.text: Cloth output +30 %, markets cost 25 % less, 30 % more fleeing craftsmen choose you.
heydays.why: The catalogue lists Chanderi and Sarangpur cloth and fine muslins among Malwa's goods; under a less warlike sultan it should consolidate and trade (adaptation).

heydays.name: Tower of Victory
heydays.text: Commanders may fight in the saka style; retinues hold 10 points longer; lords bring 20 % more men.

heydays.text: Musketeers hit 25 % harder, homeland resists conquerors 30 % longer, sea traders gather 15 % more.

burden.name: Contested succession
burden.text: Lords start one step less loyal, and legitimacy -10.
burden.why: Kingship passed among descendants of the founder chosen by electors; the catalogue lists contested successions as the first constraint and succession civil war as a failure condition.

birthright.name: Copper of the hot lands
birthright.text: Copper +40 %, forges cost 25 % less and fish +20 %.
birthright.why: The Purépecha were the leading metalworkers of Mesoamerica, working copper from the Balsas lowlands, and fished the Pátzcuaro and Cuitzeo lakes.

heydays.name: The eastern wall
heydays.text: Frontier garrisons +40 %, foot hold 8 points longer and archers hit 20 % harder.
heydays.why: A fortified eastern frontier and strong royal levies let the Purépecha defeat Axayacatl's Triple Alliance army around 1479.

heydays.name: The cazonci's seat
heydays.text: Two more officials, provinces 20 % closer to the capital, noble lords start one step more loyal and tribute +15 %.
heydays.why: Under Tzitzipandáquare (c.1454-79) power was centralised at Tzintzuntzan, with appointed governors in conquered towns.

burden.name: Three seats
burden.text: Two fewer lords before strain; provinces are 20 % further from the capital.
burden.why: Tariácuri divided the basin between three lineage centres, and the catalogue names lineage division as the Purépecha constraint.

birthright.name: Qollqa and roads
birthright.text: Stores rot 40 % less, castles feed one more ring, mountain marches 30 % faster and provinces are 20 % closer to Cusco.
birthright.why: Partly inferred: the storehouses (qollqa) and the road network grew out of highland routes around Cusco; the catalogue says they were only beginning in the 1440s.

heydays.name: Turning of the world
heydays.text: Conquests settle 30 % faster, clan chiefs start one step more loyal, Inca expansion twice as likely, with its tributary alliance option open.
heydays.why: Chronicles credit Pachacuti with saving Cusco from the Chanka and launching the empire, turning conquered lords into labour-giving allies.

heydays.name: Mit'a of the four quarters
heydays.text: Masters of works +40 %, terraces cost 30 % less and recruits refill 10 % faster.
heydays.why: In the empire after 1460-1500 subject communities worked state lands, built terraces and roads and served in armies by turn (mit'a).

heydays.name: Refuge of Vilcabamba
heydays.text: Foreign rule lasts 50 % longer in your homeland, light troops hit 30 % harder in jungle and foraging +25 %.
heydays.why: After 1536 Manco Inca and his heirs held a Neo-Inca state in the forested valleys of Vilcabamba until 1572.

burden.text: Tax reach −10 %; noble lords start one step less loyal.
burden.why: Each dead ruler's royal kin group kept his estates, and the catalogue names succession disputes on each ruler's death as an Inca constraint.
